title: State Department Launches $750 Fast-Track Visa Program in Mexico, India Still Left Waiting
excerpt: The U.S. expedited B1/B2 visa appointment pilot starts with Mexico as India’s consulates — where wait times exceed nine months — remain excluded from the program.
body:
• The U.S. State Department on July 22 named Mexico as the first country in its $750 expedited B1/B2 visa interview pilot, which promises an appointment within 10 business days.
  • India — where B1/B2 wait times at Mumbai and Hyderabad hit 9.5 months and rose 36% between May and June 2026 — has not been included among participating posts.
  • The program runs through December 31, 2026, is capped at roughly 25,000 expedited requests, and does not guarantee visa issuance.
  • Immigration attorneys say the $935 total cost ($185 standard fee plus $750 expedite fee) is prohibitively expensive for applicants in many developing countries, including India.

The U.S. State Department announced on July 22 that Mexico will be the first country to participate in its new expedited visa interview pilot program for B-1 (business) and B-2 (tourist) visa applicants. The program, which began accepting bookings on July 21 at select embassies and consulates in Mexico, allows applicants to secure an interview appointment within 10 business days for a nonrefundable fee of $750 — on top of the standard $185 visa application fee.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals stuck in months-long queues at U.S. consulates across India, the announcement offered no relief. None of India’s five consular posts — New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, or Kolkata — have been named as participating locations.

How the Pilot Works

The expedited appointment program was formalized through a Temporary Final Rule published in the Federal Register on June 9, 2026, taking effect July 1. According to Immigration Analytics, applicants first submit a DS-160 form and pay the standard $185 fee, then book a regular appointment. If their consulate participates and expedited slots remain, the system displays available appointments within 10 business days. A selected slot is held for five to 10 minutes while the applicant completes the $750 payment online.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=1TIB1gCfrS8

“The program allows applicants to receive an earlier appointment only. Every U.S. visa applicant undergoes thorough screening and vetting, and we do not issue a visa until an applicant has demonstrated to the consular officer that he or she is eligible to receive a visa under U.S. law.”

— U.S. State Department official statement

The pilot is capped at approximately 25,000 expedited requests across all participating posts through December 31, 2026, with projected revenue of roughly $19.28 million. Existing no-fee expedite mechanisms — including humanitarian requests and U.S. government referrals — remain intact.

India’s Worsening Wait Times

India’s exclusion is particularly notable given its consulates rank among the worst globally for B1/B2 backlogs. According to the State Department’s June 18 update analyzed by BAL Immigration News, wait times at most Indian posts increased by at least two months — roughly 36% — between May and June 2026.

Mumbai now faces a 9.5-month average wait with the next available appointment 10 months out. Hyderabad mirrors that at 9.5 months. New Delhi sits at 7.5 months average, with the next slot 8.5 months away. Chennai holds at 5.5 months. Kolkata, the only post to see a decrease, dropped from 4.5 to 4 months. These numbers have driven “visa shopping” — Indian applicants booking appointments at whichever consulate has the shortest line and absorbing the domestic travel cost.

Why Mexico First?

The State Department has not explained why Mexico was chosen, but the 2026 FIFA World Cup — co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico — is expected to generate extraordinary visitor visa demand. The program’s federal rule explicitly cites the World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics as design factors. The choice also arrives amid diplomatic friction: just over a week earlier, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said her government would seek legal action over Mexican citizen deaths in U.S. immigration custody, as reported by Al Jazeera.

Mexico City’s current B1/B2 wait is approximately three months — notably shorter than several Indian posts.

The Cost Question

Even if Indian consulates are eventually added, affordability is a concern. New York-based immigration attorney Michael Cataliotti told USA Today the fee is “an exorbitant amount in many of the countries where people are applying for these visas.” At current exchange rates, $935 translates to roughly ₹79,000 — a steep sum for many Indian families. The fee is nonrefundable if the applicant misses or cancels the appointment.

What Comes Next

The State Department has said it will announce additional participating posts “in phases” on travel.state.gov. The pilot’s legal framework is not limited to B1/B2 visas — expansion to other nonimmigrant categories is both legally and administratively open if demand proves sufficient, according to Immigration Analytics.

For Indian applicants, the immediate reality is unchanged: long queues, no fast-track option, and rising wait times. Whether Indian consulates make the list before the pilot expires on December 31 remains an open question — one that matters to a diaspora community accounting for a significant share of global B1/B2 demand.
nri_angle: Indian B1/B2 visa applicants face wait times of up to 10 months at consulates like Mumbai, yet India has not been named as a participating post in the $750 expedited appointment pilot, leaving hundreds of thousands of applicants without a fast-track option.
author: Diaspora Desk
